word:lxx:L700015.explanation: Abana, also called Avana, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named place or feature rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word appears once in the LXX, in 2 Kings 5:12. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense itself is simply the name Abana or Avana.

word:lxx:L700082.explanation: Ablabes means without harm—something that does not injure or hurt.

word:lxx:L700198.explanation: Slumberlessness means a state of having no sleep or being unable to sleep. It is a noun describing sleeplessness as a condition, rather than an action or a person. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs nine times, all in the deuterocanonical writings, with eight occurrences in Sirach and one in 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L700208.explanation: Anchōch, also rendered Angghokh, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the Greek Old Testament and does not carry a broader definition supplied by this record. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:45. Its precise significance belongs to the person and family setting in that passage, but the verse text is not available here for further explanation.

word:lxx:L700257.explanation: Adia is a proper name, also rendered Athia. It identifies a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, both times in genealogical material in 1 Chronicles. The available wording does not provide a separate descriptive meaning for the name, so it is best understood simply as the personal name Adia or Athia. Its precise reference is determined by the genealogy in each passage.

word:lxx:L700301.explanation: This word is a proper name, given as “Adōnai; Athone.” It identifies a named designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 1:11. The available lexical wording supplies the name itself but does not provide a broader ordinary-language definition. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, while the word’s basic function is to serve as a proper name.

word:lxx:L700374.explanation: Ἀθηνόβιος is a proper name, rendered as Athēnobios or Athinovios. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees 15, at 15:28 and 15:32. The name itself gives the person’s identity; understanding what he does or why he appears requires the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L700419.explanation: Aithiopia means Ethiopia, the name of a land.

word:lxx:L700420.explanation: This proper noun means “Aithiops” or “Ethiops,” serving as a name or designation rather than a general action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 28 times across 26 verses, so it is a recurring identifying term within that corpus. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself remains a proper name or designation. It occurs from Numbers through Zephaniah, including passages in Chronicles, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

word:lxx:L700532.explanation: This adjective means “unsettled,” describing something lacking stability, calm, or settled condition. It presents the idea of being disturbed or not firmly established, rather than secure and at rest. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 54:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a condition of instability or disturbance.

word:lxx:L700837.explanation: This proper noun refers to an Ammanite, identifying a member of the Ammanite people. It is a group name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Nehemiah. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L700868.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to someone called “Amouēl” or “Amoil.” It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:26. Because the available wording does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s identity, role, or significance. Its basic function is simply to identify an individual by name in that genealogical passage.

word:lxx:L700921.explanation: This verb means to announce—to make information known or report something to others. It describes the act of communicating a message, news, or fact rather than keeping it private. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 214 times, showing that announcing is a recurring action in many kinds of passages. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being communicated and to whom.

word:lxx:L700954.explanation: Anathōthi, also rendered Anathothi, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It appears twice in the LXX corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available information identifies the name but does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The name occurs in 1 Chronicles 11:28 and 1 Chronicles 12:3.

word:lxx:L700983.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “straighten up,” describing the action of lifting oneself from a bent or lowered posture. It presents a physical movement rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus represented here, once in Job and once in Susanna. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the act of straightening upward.

word:lxx:L701012.explanation: This word means “rejection” or “refusal.” As a noun, it describes the act of turning something down or declining to accept it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 72:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a deliberate refusal or rejection rather than simple absence or inability. The word therefore points to an expressed act of declining, opposing, or withholding acceptance.

word:lxx:L701085.explanation: This word means an “offering”: something presented or given to God. It is a noun that names the gift or presentation itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 4:19 and Psalms 50:21, showing the same central meaning in both passages. The surrounding verse determines what is offered and why, but the word itself points to the offering being presented.

word:lxx:L701250.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “measure against.” It describes assessing one thing by setting it against another measure, standard, or point of comparison. The word functions as an action, focusing on the act of weighing or comparing rather than on the object being measured. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 7:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L701269.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “act against” or “seek to counteract” someone or something. It describes active opposition rather than simple disagreement: the person using it is working against an action, plan, or opposing force. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains deliberate resistance or an attempt to prevent another purpose from succeeding.

word:lxx:L701328.explanation: Apaideutos means undisciplined, describing someone who does not love correction.

word:lxx:L701377.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “go off,” describing someone or something moving away or departing. Its basic sense is an action of leaving rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs six times in the LXX corpus, in Job, Proverbs, Hosea, and Wisdom. The surrounding sentence determines whether the departure is physical or refers more generally to being absent or removed.

word:lxx:L701575.explanation: This verb means “deal cruelly with”: it describes treating someone harshly, without kindness or consideration. As a verb, it expresses an action done to another rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 39:16. The word’s basic sense is therefore a forceful description of cruel treatment; the surrounding verse determines exactly who acts and who receives that treatment.

word:lxx:L701636.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “block up” or “stop up”—to close something so that movement or passage is prevented. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Lamentations and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and what is being closed, but its central idea remains shutting off or obstructing passage.

word:lxx:L701690.explanation: This adverb means “compactly” or “closely,” describing an action done in a tightly joined or concentrated way. It modifies another word by showing how something is arranged or carried out, rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:4. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic sense is firm: something is brought together, held, or performed closely and without looseness.

word:lxx:L701751.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to dine or have a meal. It describes the act of eating a meal rather than naming the food itself. Its stated sense includes “dine” and “each meal,” so it can refer generally to meal-eating. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 13:7. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is to dine or eat a meal.

word:lxx:L701849.explanation: This noun refers to a “chief cup-bearing” official—a person identified by responsibility for serving or bearing the cup. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 40:13, so its use is rare in this corpus. The word names an office or role rather than an action, quality, or general object. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the role functions there.

word:lxx:L701953.explanation: Asith is a proper name, preserved as “Asith” rather than translated into a descriptive word. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:33. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the name’s particular role in that verse cannot be explained further from this word entry alone. Its ordinary lexical meaning is therefore the name “Asith.”

word:lxx:L701984.explanation: This word is a proper name, presented in English as “Asouēros” or “Asoiros.” It identifies a specific named figure or subject rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 4:6. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage determine who is being named and what role that person has in the account.

word:lxx:L702079.explanation: This word means “childlessness”: the condition of having no children. As a noun, it names that state rather than describing an action. It points to a condition, not to a person, place, object, or event. In this LXX corpus, it occurs four times across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its central idea remains the absence of children, while its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L702105.explanation: Atraktos means a spindle used in needful work.

word:lxx:L702192.explanation: Apheidōs means unsparingly, or without mercy.

word:lxx:L702314.explanation: Achsan, also rendered Akhsan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Joshua 15:16 and Joshua 15:17. Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person’s designation; the surrounding verse supplies any further information about that person or the event. It should therefore be understood as a name preserved in the biblical account, not expanded into an additional concept or definition.

word:lxx:L702426.explanation: Baithmachereb, also given as Vethmakherev, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:5, so its precise referent must be understood from that passage rather than from a broad range of uses. No wider lexical sense is given beyond these name forms.

word:lxx:L702552.explanation: This adjective describes someone as “heavy” or “slow of heart,” expressing an inward dullness or heaviness rather than physical weight. It is a descriptive word for a person whose heart is not quick or responsive. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 4:3. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a heart weighed down or slow to respond. Its approved meaning is “heavy; slow of heart.”

word:lxx:L702673.explanation: This is a proper name, given as “Bēbi; Vivi.” It identifies a named person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:16. Because it is a personal name, its ordinary meaning is chiefly its identifying function; the available lexical information does not provide an additional descriptive sense or explanation of the name’s origin.

word:lxx:L702710.explanation: Bēsana, also rendered Visana, is a proper name preserved as Besana in English Bible tradition. It does not function like a common noun describing an action, quality, or object; it identifies a particular named person or location, though the available information does not establish which in Joshua 18:22. This LXX word occurs once, in Joshua 18:22, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying name rather than a broader concept.

word:lxx:L702822.explanation: “Grind” means to crush or break something by rubbing or pressing it repeatedly, and this word functions as a verb describing that action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times, each in a different verse. Its basic sense is physical and active rather than a name or description of an object. The surrounding verse determines what is being ground and how the action contributes to the sentence.

word:lxx:L702927.explanation: This verb means to drink milk. It describes the act of consuming milk as a drink, rather than naming the milk itself or a person who drinks it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: taking milk as nourishment or refreshment by drinking it.

word:lxx:L702978.explanation: This adjective describes someone as gluttonous—marked by excessive or uncontrolled appetite for food. It functions as a description rather than naming an action or object, so it characterizes a person or their conduct in terms of eating. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:7. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine precisely how the description functions there.

word:lxx:L703076.explanation: This adjective describes something as earth-like or earthy—belonging to, resembling, or arising from the earth. It presents an earthly quality rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in the Wisdom literature. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a description of earth-related character or substance.

word:lxx:L703335.explanation: This word means “sixteen,” the number that comes after fifteen and before seventeen. It functions as a number word, identifying a quantity rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:41. Its basic meaning is precise and does not require a broader symbolic sense here; the surrounding verse determines what group or quantity of sixteen is being identified.

word:lxx:L703465.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “burn through; heat to excess.” It describes intense burning or heating beyond what is ordinary, emphasizing the force or extreme degree of the heat. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 11:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is burning intensely or becoming excessively hot.

word:lxx:L703559.explanation: This verb means to reckon up items one by one—to count or enumerate them individually. It describes a deliberate process of going through a group or list and numbering its parts rather than treating everything as one undivided whole. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:6. The exact force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on careful, item-by-item counting.

word:lxx:L703560.explanation: This verb means “have full strength” or be “quite sufficient.” It describes having enough ability, strength, or resources to continue or meet a need. As a verb, it points to a condition of adequacy rather than merely possessing something. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:26; the surrounding verse is needed to determine how that basic idea applies there.

word:lxx:L703638.explanation: This word describes something interwoven with gold, emphasizing gold worked into or woven through it rather than merely placed beside it. It can function as a descriptive word for an object or material. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains “interwoven with gold.”

word:lxx:L703667.explanation: This verb means to have a way out or to break away. It describes the act of finding or making an exit rather than remaining confined or held in place. As a verb, it expresses movement toward escape or release. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 3:48. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and concrete: something or someone gets out, breaks free, or finds a means of leaving. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that action functions there.

word:lxx:L703762.explanation: This noun means “thirst,” the physical desire or need for water. In the Greek Old Testament, it names the condition of being thirsty rather than an action or a person. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Psalms, Isaiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its repeated use across these writings shows a straightforward bodily meaning, while the surrounding verse determines how the condition fits the particular statement.

word:lxx:L703906.explanation: Dōrolēmptēs means a receiver of bribes.

word:lxx:L703999.explanation: Enkyliō means to be involved in something—to be “in” it.

word:lxx:L704107.explanation: Eisagō means to lead in or bring in.

word:lxx:L704158.explanation: This verb means “beget” or “bring forth”: it describes producing or bringing someone into existence. As a verb, it points to the act of generation rather than naming the person produced. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 109:3. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its central meaning remains the act of begetting or bringing forth.

word:lxx:L704253.explanation: This verb means to redeem someone by paying a ransom. It describes release obtained through a payment made on behalf of the person being freed, emphasizing both the act of redemption and its cost. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 3:49, so its precise use there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word presents redemption as a deliberate transaction that secures release rather than merely expressing a general wish to help or rescue.

word:lxx:L704284.explanation: Ekpiptō means to fall out or fall off.

word:lxx:L704349.explanation: Ektypoō means to model or fashion something after a pattern.

word:lxx:L704370.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “outflow” or “pouring out.” It describes something being released from one place so that it flows or is poured outward. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scripture, appearing once each in Leviticus, 1 Kings, and Sirach. Its precise reference may involve different substances or situations, but its central idea remains movement outward through flowing or being poured out.

word:lxx:L704631.explanation: This noun means “outward appearance; impression”—the way something presents itself or the effect it makes on someone. It points to what is perceived from the outside, rather than necessarily describing a thing’s inner reality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is the visible or perceived impression something gives.

word:lxx:L704644.explanation: Enath is a proper name, referring to a specific place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:34. The available lexical meaning is simply “Enath,” so its significance comes from the place it identifies in that passage and its surrounding list of boundaries. This name should remain distinct as a Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a general word with several meanings.

word:lxx:L704693.explanation: This verb means “make glorious”: to bring honor, splendor, or recognized greatness to someone or something. It describes an action that causes glory to be displayed or acknowledged, rather than merely possessing glory. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures. Its use includes passages in Exodus, Ezekiel, and the Psalms, showing that the word can describe God’s acts or the honor given within human affairs.

word:lxx:L704716.explanation: This verb means “make,” describing the act of producing or carrying something out. It presents making as an action rather than as a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:40. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being made or done there, but the word itself centers on making or accomplishing something. Its single occurrence means the broader range of its use cannot be established from this corpus alone.

word:lxx:L704789.explanation: This noun means an embalmer, a person whose work is to prepare a dead body for burial by treating it so it can be preserved. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 50:2, in the account of preparing Jacob’s body. The word identifies the worker rather than the treatment itself. Its meaning is therefore a specific occupational title connected with caring for the dead after death and before burial.

word:lxx:L704877.explanation: This Greek word means “enumerate”: to count or list things one by one. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being counted, but the central idea remains a deliberate, item-by-item reckoning.

word:lxx:L704950.explanation: “Houseless” describes someone or something without a home or dwelling. It is an adjective, so it identifies a person or thing by the absence of a place to live. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 6:18. The word’s basic meaning is therefore focused and specific: being without a house or settled dwelling. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains the lack of a home.

word:lxx:L704969.explanation: Exoudenoō means to set at nought, or regard someone as of no account.

word:lxx:L705052.explanation: This verb means “laugh at” or “exult over”—to respond to another person with mocking amusement or triumphant delight. It describes an attitude expressed toward someone else, rather than ordinary laughter that is simply joyful. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:27. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic sense concerns ridiculing someone or taking pleasure in that person’s misfortune.

word:lxx:L705229.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to come to the surface or float. It describes something moving upward until it appears on top of, or remains upon, water or another surrounding substance. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 6:6. Its basic sense is a physical movement from below to the surface, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force of the word in that passage.

word:lxx:L705373.explanation: Epō means to say or speak.

word:lxx:L705492.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “dress” or “attire,” referring to clothing worn by a person. It names outward garments rather than an action or personal quality. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX material represented here, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains clothing or what someone wears.

word:lxx:L705540.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “preparation”: the act or condition of making something ready. It can describe readiness for an action, an arranged setting, or what has been made prepared. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented in this LXX corpus, including uses in Ezra, Psalms, Nahum, Zechariah, and Wisdom. Its central idea remains practical readiness rather than a specific object or event; the surrounding verse determines what is being prepared. “Preparation” is also the attested English rendering in several occurrences.

word:lxx:L705579.explanation: This adjective means “beneficent”: actively doing good and bringing helpful results to others. It describes a person, quality, or action marked by generosity and practical kindness rather than mere good intentions. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:23. Because the verse text is not provided, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding context, but its central sense remains someone or something that benefits others.

word:lxx:L705614.explanation: This adjective describes someone who can be appeased readily—that is, receptive to calming, reconciliation, or a request for peace. It presents the person as not stubbornly resistant when approached for settlement. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is someone who is easily placated or willing to be reconciled.

word:lxx:L705661.explanation: This noun means “ready obedience”: a willing, prompt response to rightful instruction or authority. It describes more than outward compliance; it emphasizes a disposition prepared to obey. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 4 Maccabees. The exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains obedience offered readily rather than reluctantly.

word:lxx:L705823.explanation: Zakanaim is a proper name, rendered also as “Zakanem.” It identifies a named location or designation in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs once, in Joshua 15:56, so its exact significance depends on the surrounding passage and the place or person being listed there. Its form functions as a name, not as a general word with a broader everyday meaning.

word:lxx:L705881.explanation: This word means “spear,” a long weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or throwing. It is a noun naming a physical weapon, and its plural form can refer to more than one spear. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah and once in Jeremiah. The word itself identifies the weapon, while the surrounding verse determines how that weapon functions in the passage. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward: a spear used as an instrument of warfare or combat.

word:lxx:L706088.explanation: Thamnathasachara is the name of a place.

word:lxx:L706123.explanation: Tharsila is a proper name, referring to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its lexical meaning is simply “Tharsila,” so it should be understood as a personal designation, not translated into a broader concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 15:14. The available information identifies the name but does not provide additional details about the person or the name’s significance in that passage.

word:lxx:L706246.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “hunt; catch.” It describes actively pursuing something with the aim of capturing it, rather than merely seeing or searching for it. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament wording represented here, at Psalms 139:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the verb. The related English rendering is “hunt,” which fits the central idea of pursuit leading to capture.

word:lxx:L706372.explanation: Iadae, also given as Iathae, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than naming an action, quality, place, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 1 Chronicles 2—at verses 28 and 32. The name itself is the word’s meaning here; no further ordinary-language definition or name-meaning is provided. Its precise reference in each genealogy depends on the surrounding verse text.

word:lxx:L706422.explanation: Ianoka is a proper name, rendered as “Ianōka; Ianoka.” It identifies a particular named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 16:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal or place-name designation.

word:lxx:L706527.explanation: Ieddouran, also rendered Ieththuran, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 8:10. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional meaning or description of the person. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L706664.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Iesou” or “Iesu.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Numbers 26:28. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the name’s specific referent in that passage cannot be clarified further here. Its basic function is simply to name an individual.

word:lxx:L706725.explanation: This verb means “refresh”: to restore freshness, strength, or renewed vitality. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action done to something or someone, rather than a person or object itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek text of Sirach, appearing once in Sirach 35:8 and once in Sirach 43:22. Its basic meaning remains focused and consistent: bringing renewal or relief so that what has been affected becomes fresh again. The surrounding verse determines whether the refreshing concerns a person, condition, or created thing.

word:lxx:L706826.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “equal to the gods” or “godlike.” It expresses resemblance to divine beings or a status viewed as comparable to theirs, rather than naming a god itself.
